candidates.attacker_control: The original request URI/query string is attacker-controlled. The rewrite documentation explicitly permits inserting any character in %nn form (webapps/docs/rewrite.xml:59-79), and ResolverImpl's %{REQUEST_URI}/%{THE_REQUEST} variables return the raw, un-normalised request URI (ResolverImpl.java:118-121), which can still contain %2e%2e when the normalised path no longer does. A rule whose substitution incorporates such data (or a map that unescapes) can therefore place %2e/%2f into the rewrite output under client influence. I did not find a purely client-driven path with the default/typical rules.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that (a) RewriteValve does call RequestUtil.normalize and that StandardRoot.validate()/AbstractFileResourceSet.file() re-normalise and canonicalise resource paths (mitigating much of the impact); (b) step 1 of the RewriteValve encoding pipeline (encodeForRewrite, lines 868-892) re-encodes literal '%' as %25, which blocks the straightforward client path injection of %2e via the mapped URL; (c) the recently fixed issues in the same areas are present (AbstractResourceSet.setWebAppMount/isPathMounted for CVE-2025-49125/69717, DirResourceSet CVE-2024-56337 canonical-cache checks, allowPartialPut + ContentRange.isValid for CVE-2025-24813, maxPartCount=50/maxPartHeaderSize limits for the multipart DoS fix, JNDIRealm doFilterEscaping, WebdavServlet isSpecialPath/WebdavResolver, CsrfPreventionFilter enforce=true, NetMask/UDecoder/Http11InputBuffer checks). This may simply be long-standing upstream design rather than a regression.
candidates.impact: Potential access to resources outside the intended request path (information disclosure), bypass of the /WEB-INF and /META-INF direct-access restrictions in StandardContextValve, and, when a write-enabled default servlet/WebDAV is present, potential creation/modification of files outside the intended path. Because StandardRoot.validate() and AbstractFileResourceSet.file() perform their own normalisation and canonical-path containment checks, the practical impact is bounded by whether the denormalised segments survive to those layers; I could not demonstrate end-to-end traversal from source alone.
candidates.prerequisites: RewriteValve enabled and configured with at least one rule whose substitution can contain encoded dot segments (e.g., literal %2e%2e, or data from %{REQUEST_URI}/a rewrite map), and a request that reaches the valve. No authentication is required for the traversal itself; impact depends on what the target web application serves (e.g., default servlet, WebDAV, static resources, or a write-enabled DefaultServlet for JSP/class writes).
candidates.root_cause: In RewriteValve.invoke() the rewritten path is normalised while still percent-encoded (RequestUtil.normalize(urlStringRewriteEncoded), line 558) and only afterwards URL-decoded (URLDecoder.decode(urlStringRewriteEncoded, uriCharset), line 565). Any %2e/%2f sequences present in the rewrite output therefore become '.', '..' and '/' only after normalisation. The valve then re-enters CoyoteAdapter.postParseRequest via prepare(); because requestURI()/decodedURI() were set as chars, the char/String branch runs (CoyoteAdapter.java:653-667) and, per its own comment, assumes decodedURI is already 'decoded and normalized' and only calls decodedURI.toChars(). No further normalisation is applied before Mapper.map() (CoyoteAdapter.java:695-697), so mappingData.requestPath, servletPath/pathInfo (and hence getRelativePath() in Default/WebdavServlet and getRequestPathMB() in StandardContextValve) can be derived from a denormalised path.
candidates.title: RewriteValve decodes the rewritten path after normalising it, so the decoded URI handed to the mapper can retain dot-segments (normalisation invariant violated in CoyoteAdapter's char-type branch)
candidates.trace: request -> CoyoteAdapter.postParseRequest decodes and normalises the original URI (lines 636-652) -> RewriteValve matches a rule and builds urlStringRewriteEncoded -> line 558 normalises while the string is still encoded (no '..' visible) -> line 565 URL-decodes, introducing real '/' and '..' -> requestURI (encoded) and decodedURI (denormalised) are set (lines 547-565) -> request.getMappingData().recycle()+recycleSessionInfo() (582-583) -> adapter.prepare() re-enters postParseRequest -> char-type branch only calls decodedURI.toChars() (CoyoteAdapter 666) -> Mapper.map(serverName, decodedURI, ...) (697) maps a denormalised path -> wrapped servlet derives servletPath/pathInfo (DefaultServlet.getRelativePath, lines 469-500) and StandardContextValve's /WEB-INF//META-INF prefix check (lines 62-68) evaluates the denormalised request path.
candidates.unverified: No runtime test or exploit was attempted; I could not construct a request that produces '%2e' in the rewrite output without a specific (non-default) rewrite configuration; I could not diff this snapshot against the upstream fixed version to confirm the ordering was changed by a later security fix; the P1 index is partial (1913/2935 Java files parsed, 96 files missing) and control/data-flow/reachability were not modelled.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper path normalisation leading to potential path traversal / restriction bypass (CWE-22, CWE-180)

coverage_summary: Scope: 3031 source files under the assigned root (main sources/config of Apache Tomcat 10.1.43-dev plus modules and webapps); 1913 Java files indexed by the P1 index (partial: 96 source files missing from the index; no control-flow/data-flow/reachability modelling). I read and cross-checked the request pipeline (CoyoteAdapter, Request/Parameters, Http11InputBuffer/Processor, UDecoder, ContentRange), web resource layer (StandardRoot, AbstractResourceSet, Dir/File/AbstractArchiveResourceSet), servlets (Default/Webdav/CGI/Jsp), security components (StandardContextValve, AuthenticatorBase, RealmBase/JNDIRealm, CsrfPreventionFilter, CorsFilter, Rate/CIDR/RequestFilter valves, NetMask), RewriteValve, HTTP/2 handler/parser samples, conf/web.xml, manager/host-manager descriptors and JSPs, SSI, WebSocket UriTemplate, and the mapping/security-constraint classes. Unreviewed/unchecked: TLS/JSSE/OpenSSL internals, tribes/cluster internals, most of dbcp2 and jdbc-pool, JMX/modeler, JSP compiler internals beyond spot checks, and the 96 unindexed files; no tests exist in the snapshot and nothing was executed.
limitations: No runtime verification, exploit attempt, or build/test execution was performed (tools are read-only; code execution is out of scope).
No access to upstream history/patches or CVE labels, so I could not confirm whether the RewriteValve ordering is a deviation from a later fixed version.
The P1 relation index is partial and syntactic only (no data-flow/control-flow/reachability); index absence is not evidence of safety, and index facts were not treated as findings.
HTTP/2, TLS, clustering, JMX and DBCP areas were only sampled; a flaw could exist there.
The candidate's exploitation is configuration-dependent and I could not construct a purely client-controlled path from source, so it should be treated as a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The snapshot has no test tree, removing an important source of behavioural evidence.

rejected_leads.reason: The fix appears present: AbstractResourceSet.setWebAppMount applies checkPath and strips trailing '/', isPathMounted enforces the '/' boundary, and DirResourceSet/AbstractArchiveResourceSet use it for getResource/mkdir/write.

Connector defaults maxPartCount=50, maxPartHeaderSize=512, and Request.parseParts computes the lower of the parameter- and part-based limits and enforces fileCountMax/partHeaderSizeMax; no bypass identified.
DirResourceSet.initInternal still refuses to start a writable set when the JVM canonical-name cache cannot be disabled, and AbstractFileResourceSet.file() rejects case/alias mismatches.
getUserBySearch applies doFilterEscaping(username) before MessageFormat substitution.
SSIServlet/SSIFilter default allowExec=false and only register the exec command when enabled.
webapps/manager/WEB-INF/web.xml still enforces manager-gui/script/jmx/status constraints, META-INF/context.xml restricts to localhost, and manager JSP output uses JspHelper.escapeXml.
isSpecialPath checks cover service/doPut/delete/copy/destination, and WebdavResolver returns a dummy InputSource for external entities.

rejected_leads.lead: HTTP/2 stream/memory DoS or padding/content-length handling
rejected_leads.reason: Padding is validated and subtracted before receivedData, content-length consistency is enforced, overhead-count mitigations and closed-stream pruning (5x maxConcurrentStreams) are present; no concrete unbounded growth identified from source.

summary: Apache Tomcat 10.1.43-dev source snapshot (main sources only; no test tree, ~3031 files). I reviewed the request path, path-normalisation, resource-serving, authentication/authorisation, filter, rewrite and connector code, and verified that the recent hardening around this snapshot is present (CVE-2024-50379/56337 canonical-cache checks, CVE-2025-24813 partial-PUT/allowPartialPut + ContentRange validation, CVE-2025-49125 pre/post-resource mount checks and the 69717 regression fix, multipart part/parameter limits, JNDI LDAP filter escaping, WebDAV special-path and XXE protections, SSI exec disabled by default, manager constraints). The single strongest source-evidenced issue I found is a cross-file normalisation-invariant violation in the RewriteValve/CoyoteAdapter boundary: RewriteValve normalises the rewritten path while it is still percent-encoded and only then URL-decodes it, after which CoyoteAdapter's char-type branch explicitly assumes a decoded *and normalised* URI and performs no further normalisation before mapping. That can leave dot-segments in the decoded URI handed to the mapper, which is the input used for servlet/wrapper selection, getRequestPathMB() (/WEB-INF and /META-INF checks) and DefaultServlet/WebdavServlet path resolution. The issue is configuration-dependent (a rewrite rule must emit encoded dot/separator sequences) and I could not demonstrate a purely client-controlled path, so I submit it only as a low-confidence lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
